title: I Weep for You, If Weeping Could Quench My Thirst
intro: Al-Sharif al-Radi mourns his mother Fatima bint al-Nasir, whose death the diwan dates to Dhu al-Hijja 385 AH (995–996 CE). He moves from the tears he conceals in public to the practical help and prayers she once gave him. At the grave he calls for rain, then claims the duty of watering it for his own tears. In the last verse he remembers whose body first carried his.

translation: I weep for you, if weeping could quench my thirst,
and speak, if words could carry off my sickness.
1.sharh: He can still weep and speak to her. Each act comes with an impossible condition. His own tears supply the water in the first image, yet the thirst is his own too.

translation: I take refuge in patient endurance for comfort,
if patient endurance held any comfort for me.
2.sharh: “Beautiful patience”, a Qur’anic expression associated with Jacob’s grief for Joseph, gives him words to live by. Saying them twice exposes how little ease they bring him.

translation: At times my tears are too many for me,
at others I take shelter in my dignity and shame.
3.sharh: The verb makes a contest of numbers out of a struggle with tears. Against so many of them he can call on only two resources, pride and the reluctance to be seen.

translation: How many tears I disguised with my fingertips
and hid in my cloak to keep up appearances.
4.sharh: The fingers work close to the eye and the cloak screens the face. By describing those small movements he lets his mother see what no one present was meant to notice.

translation: I show my enemy a steady face. If he knew
how I writhe, my enemies would have their fill of it.
5.sharh: His discomposure would furnish a cure for his enemies’ spite. It is the first cure anyone in the poem might actually obtain.

translation: I would hold back no treasure to ransom you,
if ransom ever brought a dead person back.
6.sharh: A ransom ordinarily requires someone empowered to hand the captive back. His readiness to pay only brings out the absence of anyone with whom he might bargain.

translation: Had strength been able to ward off this death,
companies of men would have massed behind my standard,
7.sharh: He tries the other resource available to a man of standing. The standard gives the gathering troops a visible centre, but their entire muster takes place inside an “if”.

translation: with men schooled in combat who took
the shade of spears for shelter on every day of battle.
8.sharh: The spears are overhead like a canopy. Finding shade under them measures how completely these men are at home in what others would experience as danger.

translation: When their eyes grow sore in the hollows they cross by night,
they line them with the dark’s own antimony.
9.sharh: Antimony powder darkens the rims of the eyes and was also applied medicinally. Their treatment for eyes sore from riding through the dark is another dose of darkness.

translation: They walk in rings of mail like
solid boulders in a pool of water,
10.sharh: Through the rippling rings one glimpses the weight of their bodies. A pool offers the peculiar combination the comparison needs, moving reflections over stones that hold firm.

translation: with lightning from armour, thunder from blades,
clouds of dust and a downpour of blood.
11.sharh: A storm assembles feature by feature, from the glint of a cuirass to the clang of blades. Dust supplies the cloud and the result of the fighting supplies its rain.

translation: For you I have lost my self-command and composure.
For you I have forgotten my pride and defiance.
12.sharh: After the imaginary host comes the one person for whom all his defences fail. The same small phrase, “for you”, occupies the same place in both halves.

translation: I have done what dents the dignity of its doer,
such searing anguish came upon me.
13.sharh: Dignity acquires an edge that can be chipped. He leaves the act that cost him his composure unnamed, allowing the sounds of the next verse to disclose it.

translation: How often a sob ebbed into a groan
and I finished it by drawing one long breath.
14.sharh: The noises follow the course of a single breath. Its first force fails, a low moan takes over, and the lungs must draw again to finish what they started.

translation: Distraught, I leap in the snares of a grief
that has mastered my endurance and strength.
15.sharh: A trapped creature can still spring, and may do so all the more furiously for being caught. The image gives him plenty of movement and no means of escape.

translation: Time has gone about its customary tricks,
overturning my hopes, reversing what I longed for.
16.sharh: He speaks of time as an old hand at this business. The two expressions for reversal prepare an exact exchange of places between mother and son.

translation: I had hoped to be the ransom that spared you
what overtook you. Instead you were my ransom.
17.sharh: The identical word for ransom changes owners in mid-verse. Her death did not literally purchase his life, but his survival makes the exchange feel terribly exact.

translation: Separation is hard even for strangers grown dear.
How then can close kin bear to part?
18.sharh: He invites assent to a modest case before turning to his own. People once strangers can hardly bear to part, and his bond with her began before he was born.

translation: The world has the ways of a woman who sells herself,
now holding back, now giving.
19.sharh: The harsh comparison gives fortune a face and an intention. Her alternation of favours and refusals lets the bereaved son address an injury as though someone had deliberately dealt it.

translation: At times she meets you with affection like your own.
Then she greets you with hatred, a stranger to you.
20.sharh: The world first returns the look she is given. Then her expression alters so much that an encounter with the same familiar person feels like meeting a stranger.

translation: The days wear us away as they take their turns,
as the bucket rope frays against the sides of a well.
21.sharh: A rope drawn against the rim loses a little of itself on every journey. The repeated contact makes the slow action of one day after another visible.

translation: A whole long life seems one evening halt to a rider
who rests off his weariness and presses on by night.
22.sharh: He measures a lifetime by a traveller’s break towards evening. Once the fatigue has passed, even this apparently long stay proves a brief interval before the night ride.

translation: You spent your life in chastity and abstinence
and were laid down heavy with burdens,
23.sharh: The rider’s brief halt gives way to the mother’s choices over a whole lifetime. The printed verb, “you wore thin”, carries the tired mount into this verse. The burdens she bore emerge as fasting and night prayer in the next.

translation: fasting through summer days beneath a blazing sun,
standing through the whole of the dark night in prayer.
24.sharh: Heat is what makes this particular fast demanding. At the other end of the day, standing for prayer fills the hours that would ordinarily allow her to recover.

translation: No one ever struck a losing bargain
buying the ease of the gardens with a life of hardship.
25.sharh: The language of exchange returns. The son could name no acceptable ransom for her, but he believes her privations have already bought the ease of paradise.

translation: Were every devoted mother such as you,
her sons could do with her alone, without their fathers.
26.sharh: He measures her by the work she actually did in the household. The startling claim about fathers is followed by memories of the protection, money and nursing she provided.

translation: How could I forget, when wherever my glance falls
some lasting sign of your goodness faces me?
27.sharh: Her goodness has left objects or people he can still see. To avoid the reminders that defeat consolation he would have to give up looking at his surroundings altogether.

translation: Good deeds of yours bring gladness to my eyes
and so become the surest bringers of my tears.
28.sharh: To cool someone’s eye is to give them joy. The eye glad at what she accomplished is precisely the eye that floods at the thought of who accomplished it.

translation: One who has put off life has never died
while their good deeds count their name among the living.
29.sharh: Life can be taken off like a garment. The reckoning of the living has another entry for her, however, supplied by the people who still benefit from what she did.

translation: Behind whose hand can I now find shelter
from the turns of calamity? Whose prayer protects me?
30.sharh: Her hand and her prayer once belonged to the same stock of protection. The questions measure what remains missing even while her name is still alive.

translation: Who will supply me when my means run short?
Who will nurse me through illness?
31.sharh: The two helpers have closely patterned names in Arabic. He can distinguish the tasks of providing money and tending the sick more easily than he can distinguish the person who performed them.

translation: Who, when disaster sprang upon me,
used to shield me from harm?
32.sharh: Calamity springs like an assailant already within reach. The past “used to” makes protection a matter of repeated experience, even as the question seeks someone for the future.

translation: Who will draw the covering of their prayer over me,
a sanctuary from hardship and hurt?
33.sharh: Her prayer was a curtain she could let down around him. Inside it he stood on the equivalent of sanctuary ground, where one who took refuge had a claim to protection.

translation: Two losses go on renewing themselves
for all time, her dying and my living on.
34.sharh: He alters the arithmetic of bereavement. There has been one death, but each morning gives him the double fact of her absence and his presence to experience again.

translation: Everyone bears witness to her nobility,
on the evidence of the children she bore.
35.sharh: His siblings enter the poem as evidence in a public judgement. What observers can see in her children allows them to testify about the mother who raised them.

translation: In the dark of every crisis, in every strait,
the mark of her generous hand comes clear.
36.sharh: A “white hand” is an Arabic expression for a benefaction. Giving the crisis actual darkness allows that familiar expression to take on visible brightness again.

translation: She laid up a good name for us that will outlast
what fathers lay by for their children.
37.sharh: Both kinds of inheritance are described by the same verb for storing something away. The family will be able to draw on her reputation long after more tangible legacies run out.

translation: I had hoped my own day would come before hers.
She dreaded being left behind me.
38.sharh: What he hoped for out of love she feared for the very same reason. Each wanted to spare the other the place the son now occupies.

translation: Many who bid me bear up stir my sickness,
thinking that this is my medicine.
39.sharh: Consolers have to bring his loss to mind to urge him to bear it. Their good intentions make them agents of the very illness introduced in the opening verse.

translation: I take refuge in cool shade and seem
in my burning to take refuge on sun-scorched ground.
40.sharh: The shelter stays cool for anyone else who might stand there. He carries the source of heat with him, so the same verb for taking refuge lands him on blistering earth.

translation: I start up from sweet sleep in terror,
as a man stung by venom recoils from dozing.
41.sharh: Sleep, the other available refuge, proves as unreliable as shade. The sting supplies a bodily comparison for the sudden violent start that grief can produce in a sleeping person.

translation: Your illustrious forebears, through whom
springs of blessings welled up,
42.sharh: A change of scale takes us from a man’s broken sleep to several generations. Their gifts are figured as springs, whose benefit continues to flow beyond their source.

translation: some champions of right, some calling others
to paths of guidance, some lifting deep distress,
43.sharh: The blessings take three human forms, upholding right, guiding others and relieving distress. “Champion of right” also recalls al-Nasir li’l-Haqq, a title borne by an ancestor of Fatima.

translation: took their station on the very crest of glory’s hump,
above shoulders and backs alike.
44.sharh: The summit of a camel’s hump provides a precise point of elevation. Shoulders and backs spread out below it, giving the conventional idea of high lineage a physical landscape.

translation: Each had hands that raced each other to give
and set sound words and judgements straight.
45.sharh: A man’s own two hands compete to be first to give. The settled accuracy of his judgement supplies a different quality from sheer speed in generosity.

translation: Even under his sharp gaze one hopes for generosity.
Even with his head and eyes lowered one fears him.
46.sharh: The visitor cannot read a simple promise or threat from the ancestor’s face. Even the keen look leaves room for hope, and even lowered eyes command respect.

translation: They passed on in the footsteps of earlier peoples,
leaving well-trodden roads to honour behind them.
47.sharh: They too had predecessors and had to follow them out of life. Their descendants inherit something actively usable, a road others have already made passable.

translation: O grave to which I give my love, if only
the tears of every sky could pour themselves out on it.
48.sharh: Address passes to the grave that now contains her. His two eyes could never supply the water he wishes for it, so he endows the heavens themselves with eyes to drain.

translation: May a thunder-chanting cloud go on resounding,
its lightning lively, its clamour rising,
49.sharh: The customary wish for rain over a grave becomes a sustained description of the arriving cloud. The Arabic lends it the rhythms of chanted verse alongside the more obvious roar of thunder.

translation: lowing like an old camel harried by night travel,
heaving like a she-camel heavy with young,
50.sharh: The thunder has the voice of a burdened old male camel. For the way the cloud moves, the comparison changes animals and gives it the weight of a female close to giving birth.

translation: drawing laden clouds behind it as though
they carried tangled dunes and ridges of sand,
51.sharh: One cloud draws a whole file of others. Their burden is invisible until he compares it with something whose immense weight the desert traveller can see, entire ridges of sand.

translation: urging them on in the dark wing of night, driving
those slow movers with a headlong wind.
52.sharh: Water makes these clouds valuable and also makes them slow. The driving wind answers both needs of the prayer, an ample fall of rain that will reach the grave soon.

translation: Its lightning flings you chunks of life-giving rain
and breaks open chests of dew for you,
53.sharh: Rain falls in substantial pieces and dew comes packed like a merchant’s precious goods. The formal opening of the containers makes the grave the recipient of an offering.

translation: drawing milk from the untouched store of every cloud
that feeds fresh shoots in a meadow still ungrazed.
54.sharh: The milk drawn from a cloud becomes food for the first grass. The same adjective, “untouched”, travels from the rain-bearing cloud to a meadow on which no animal has yet grazed.

translation: I would be mean indeed if I failed to water her with tears
and left her watering to the rising and setting stars.
55.sharh: The stars marked the seasons in which rain was expected. His elaborate appeal to the weather suddenly sounds to him like passing on a duty that belongs to her son.

translation: My grief for those I left behind,
a layer of desert earth laid over them.
56.sharh: Beneath the sky he has just imagined lies the flat, heavy covering of earth. Grief expands to include other buried loved ones, while the description narrows to what has happened to their faces.

translation: Faces I begrudged other eyes even a glimpse of,
I have come to load with fine dust.
57.sharh: Before, he would hardly allow another person a glance at those faces. In recalling the burial he has to see himself as one of the hands that covered them.

translation: Eyes whose lids the soil has lined with kohl
I once guarded against every speck of grit.
58.sharh: Kohl ordinarily beautifies or soothes the eye. Earth now performs that intimate service on lids he once guarded from so much as a speck.

translation: Their tombs lie close at hand for visitors.
To those who seek them they are far, so far away.
59.sharh: A visitor and a seeker can be the same person. Getting to the grave is the easy part, and arriving there brings home how distant its occupant is.

translation: How grievous what there, in their very homes,
meets the listening ear and seeing eye.
60.sharh: He gives a grave the expression for the heart of someone’s home. A caller who attends with both ear and eye receives little of the welcome those words ordinarily promise.

translation: Your great kindness keeps you company
when night brings the desolation of the dusty earth.
61.sharh: The plural graves give way again to the one woman. Each kindness she once did for someone else can now come back to her as a companion through the dark.

translation: The brightness of the good you sent ahead
takes the place of lights for you in darkness.
62.sharh: She had in effect sent provisions on ahead. After the companion he has imagined for her comes a source of light furnished by the very things she did while alive.

translation: May the One your deeds delighted go on
gladdening you with His mercy, morning and evening.
63.sharh: The verb for giving pleasure first takes God as its object and then his mother. His mercy enters late in the Arabic sentence, as the gift the son prays will outlast each change of day.

translation: May He bless you, as His blessing attended you
before your death, and richly reward you.
64.sharh: The blessing crosses the boundary of death. He stops short of naming a particular reward, using an expression of wonder at its magnitude.

translation: If the flat grave-stones could carry you my messages,
or earth could make you hear my call,
65.sharh: Stones and earth are the obstacles between speaker and listener. His wish gives them the opposite office for a moment, as carriers of the words this poem has addressed to her.

translation: you would hear how long I groan and grieve
and know how well I have cared and kept faith.
66.sharh: The answer to the preceding “if” is delayed across the verse break. What he wants her to receive includes the evidence of care, an assurance that matters as much as the noise of grief.

translation: My kicking once inside your body set in motion
the grief for you that now kicks deep in mine.
67.sharh: The last line reaches further back than either of their memories together. The same words for kicking and for the body’s interior exchange owners, making the son’s present grief answer his first movements inside her.

1.1.3.meaning: To slake thirst. His burning grief is the thirst he tries to quench.

2.1.2-3.head: الصَّبر الجَميل
2.1.2-3.meaning: “Beautiful patience”, enduring affliction with restraint, a phrase Jacob uses in the Qur’an (12.18 and 12.83).

3.2.3.head: أُكرومَة
3.2.3.meaning: A quality of nobility or self-respect that checks a public display of grief.

4.1.3.head: مَوَّهَ
4.1.3.meaning: To disguise what something is, here by brushing away the evidence of a tear.

5.2.1.head: تَمَلمُل
5.2.1.meaning: Restlessness that makes it hard to hold still.

6.1.6.head: رَغيبَة
6.1.6.meaning: A prized possession that its owner would ordinarily be slow to part with.

8.1.3.head: قِراع
8.1.3.meaning: The exchange of blows in close combat.

9.1.3.head: مَرِهَ
9.1.3.meaning: To have sore, inflamed eyes, traditionally associated with going without kohl.

9.1.4-5.head: أَغباب السُّرى
9.1.4-5.meaning: “The recesses of night travel”, the dark folds of ground crossed by night, also understood more generally as the hardships of night marches.

9.2.3.head: إِثمِد
9.2.3.meaning: Ithmid, the dark mineral ground to make kohl for the eyes.

11.2.2.head: قَسطَلَة
11.2.2.meaning: A mass of dust raised by moving horses.

13.2.5.head: البُرَحاء
13.2.5.meaning: The extremity of pain or distress.

14.2.3.head: الصُّعَداء
14.2.3.meaning: A long, deep breath or sigh under distress.

15.1.4.head: حَبائِل
15.1.4.meaning: Snares or nooses laid for game.

15.2.4.head: غَناء
15.2.4.meaning: Capacity or resourcefulness in the face of a task.

19.1.4.head: مومِس
19.1.4.meaning: A woman who sells sex, invoked here for the giving and withholding of favours.

21.2.2.head: الرِّشاء
21.2.2.meaning: The rope by which a bucket is lowered and drawn up.

21.2.4.head: أَرجاء
21.2.4.meaning: The sides or margins, here the sides of the well against which the rope rubs.

22.1.4.head: رَوحَة
22.1.4.meaning: An evening stage or respite on a journey, here a measure of life’s brevity.

22.2.2.head: اللُّغوب
22.2.2.meaning: Weariness or exhaustion after sustained exertion.

22.2.5.head: إِسراء
22.2.5.meaning: Night travel, resumed once the rider has recovered.

23.1.1.head: أَمضى
23.1.1.meaning: To spend or pass one’s time. The probable sung reading is amdayti. The two printed editions and the caption have andayti (أنضيتِ), “you wore thin”, as a long journey wears out a mount.

24.2.4.head: اللَّيلاء
24.2.4.meaning: Deeply dark, an intensifying adjective for the night.

25.1.4.head: غَبين
25.1.4.meaning: Someone who has come off badly in a transaction.

27.2.4.head: إِزاء
27.2.4.meaning: Directly opposite or in front of one.

28.1.3-4.head: قَرَّتِ العَين
28.1.3-4.meaning: “My eyes grow cool”, an idiom for the joy and satisfaction something gives.

29.1.4-5.head: نَزَعَ البَقاء
29.1.4-5.meaning: “Took off life”, a figure for dying that allows a good name to survive the casting off.

30.1.3.head: اِستَجَنَّ
30.1.3.meaning: To take cover or put oneself under protection.

31.2.2.head: مُعَلِّل
31.2.2.meaning: Someone who tends and comforts a sick person.

32.1.4.head: ساوَرَ
32.1.4.meaning: To spring upon someone or close with an adversary.

33.1.3.head: لَطَّ
33.1.3.meaning: To let a covering down over someone.

33.2.1.head: حَرَم
33.2.1.meaning: Sanctuary, a place where one who takes refuge enjoys protection.

36.2.4-5.head: اليَد البَيضاء
36.2.4-5.meaning: “The white hand”, a benefaction whose effect is apparent to others.

38.2.1.head: يَوم
38.2.1.meaning: His day of death, with death itself left unstated.

40.2.4.head: الرَّمضاء
40.2.4.meaning: Ground or stones baked hot by the sun.

41.2.2.head: لَديغ
41.2.2.meaning: A person bitten by a snake or stung by a scorpion.

43.1.2-3.head: ناصِرٌ لِلحَقّ
43.1.2-3.meaning: “Champion of right”, also the title al-Nasir li’l-Haqq borne by Fatima’s ancestor al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Utrush.

43.2.5.head: الغَمّاء
43.2.5.meaning: Distress so enveloping that relief is hidden from view.

44.1.2.head: عَرعَرَة
44.1.2.meaning: The highest point of something, here the crest of a camel’s hump.

44.2.3.head: أَثباج
44.2.3.meaning: The broad or upper parts of backs.

46.2.4.head: إِغضاء
46.2.4.meaning: Lowering the eyelids, sometimes as a sign of forbearance.

49.1.3.head: مُرتَجِز
49.1.3.meaning: One chanting verse in rajaz metre, here a cloud chanting with its thunder.

50.1.4.head: جَعجَعَ
50.1.4.meaning: To hem in or drive hard, here the effect of a night’s journey.

50.2.4.head: عُشَراء
50.2.4.meaning: A she-camel ten months into pregnancy and heavy with young.

51.2.2.head: عَقَدات
51.2.2.meaning: Masses of sand accumulated into mounds.

51.2.3.head: أَنقاء
51.2.3.meaning: Long ridges or dunes of sand.

53.1.3-4.head: أَفلاذ الحَيا
53.1.3-4.meaning: “Pieces of life-giving rain”, with a word ordinarily used of substantial cuts of flesh.

53.2.1.head: فَضَّ
53.2.1.meaning: To break a seal and open what it protects, here a case imagined full of precious dew.

53.2.3.head: لَطائِم
53.2.3.meaning: Cases of costly merchandise or perfume, whose seals are broken to release their contents.

54.1.1.head: مُتَحَلِّب
54.1.1.meaning: Drawing out a cloud’s water as one draws milk from an udder. Dar Sadir prints mutahalliyan, “adorning himself”.

54.2.2.head: جَميم
54.2.2.meaning: The first low, fresh growth of herbage.

55.2.4.head: أَنواء
55.2.4.meaning: Anwa’, star settings and risings by which the Arabs reckoned seasons of rain.

56.2.4.head: بَيداء
56.2.4.meaning: Open desert, here the earth covering the dead. The reciter says al-sahba’, red wine, the rhyme of the following printed verse, which he skips.

57.2.2.head: أَوقَرَ
57.2.2.meaning: To load something heavily, here with the earth thrown into the grave.

57.2.4.head: البَوغاء
57.2.4.meaning: Fine loose dust or powdery soil.

58.2.5.head: أَقذاء
58.2.5.meaning: Specks of dirt or chaff that irritate the eye.

60.1.4-5.head: عُقر الدّار
60.1.4-5.meaning: “The heart of their homes”, the innermost place where they dwell, here their graves.

63.1.6.head: زالَ
63.1.6.meaning: In a prayer for the continuance of mercy. The reciter uses a feminine verb anticipating “His mercy”. The Dar Sadir text has a masculine verb.

65.1.4.head: صَفيح
65.1.4.meaning: Broad, flat stones laid over a grave.

67.1.2.head: اِرتِكاض
67.1.2.meaning: The kicking of an unborn child. The same root gives grief its movement in the son.
